doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

chapter: Michael, influences and the Brecker Brothers
title: Writing the first album as a daily craft
summary: Inspired by Truman Capote, he wrote daily, notating rhythms and making cassette demos until nine tunes existed.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you, you mentioned when you were trying to articulate that thing you said yeah I can’t even do this anymore. I wondered if at the time — it’s a two part question. First of all the rhythms of the melodies and the whole band, did you have to spend a lot of time figuring out how to notate those things? Was it a chore? [Scats]

Well it was a craft that’s the way I looked at it. And once again it came from an interview. I saw, when I was starting to do this Truman Capote was interviewed, the great writer on one of the talk shows. And he was — I’m always interested in other artists’ thought process or work process. And he spent a little time in his interview talking about just the craft of writing books, writing literature. The fact that you just have to sit down and do it every day. So it’s not — he didn’t wait for inspiration. And I think Hemingway was similar. He would write — most writers sit down and do it every day. So I took that to mind and I just spent time sitting at a keyboard or various keyboards and to answer your question, yes writing every note down, trying to figure out the rhythms correctly on score paper. Like everyone this was way before all the electronics. Pencil and paper and score paper and I’d have to figure out all the rhythms and voice everything. And spend time. Sometimes I came up with nothing but the whole thing was that I did spend an hour or two or three every day just sitting there writing stuff, transferring it to cassette tapes — I had the idea of bouncing — I didn’t have a four track yet — ping ponging. So I’d record on one cassette player then record over it on another one. I’d lose a lot of whatever the word is.
Yeah. You’re not the only one.

Yeah. So that’s how eventually by doing that for months at a time over a year I ended up with the nine tunes written relatively correctly. I had my own kind of harmonic ear thing. Because there were still blanks in my music education that I eventually kind of filled up some holes but that’s part of the charm of some of that music. The something over something, I didn’t know how to figure out some of the scales — they were really melodic minor scales — modes really that I discovered later. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
